F5.rationale: F5 is the load-bearing path and §2.1's HNDL-for-signed-artifacts argument is the load-bearing thesis. My honest update after live-research: the TNFL (Trust Now, Forge Later, originally STFT — Sign Today, Forge Tomorrow, 2018) literature is REAL, NAMED, and discussed in industry (PQShield 'Harvest-Now-Forge-Later'; postquantum.com; EverTrust; NIST circles; the Josefsson-2024 SPHINCS+-for-git proposal explicitly motivated by long-term verification). My strongest counter — 'no documented case' — is true but symmetric (HNDL-for-encryption also has no documented realized attack pre-CRQC). My second counter — 'easier CRQC targets exist' — survives partially but doesn't refute the class. My third counter — 'argument proves too much, git/Sigstore/Filecoin/Arweave don't panic' — IS the strongest surviving objection, and the §2.1 draft DOES NOT engage with it (Lens 15 will hit this too). VERDICT: pursue F5 but the §2.1 draft as written is structurally vulnerable on the proves-too-much axis and must be revised before publication. See `hndl_for_sigs_argument_survival` field.

hndl_for_sigs_argument_survival: PARTIAL SURVIVAL. My strongest counter going in — 'TNFL is speculative; no documented case; we don't see git/Sigstore panicking' — collapses on its first claim (TNFL is a NAMED industry-recognized threat class with 8 years of literature: STFT 2018 → TNFL 2023+ → PQShield 'Harvest-Now-Forge-Later' 2024+; multiple PQC industry firms publish on it as an established class). My second claim (no documented realized attack) is true but symmetric with HNDL-for-encryption, which Benten accepts; the symmetry asymmetry doesn't hold. BUT my third claim — 'argument proves too much; git commits, Sigstore, Filecoin/Arweave permaweb, Debian sigs, all have decade+ persistence + classical sigs + no panic' — DOES survive and is the unresolved hole in §2.1. The paragraph asserts content-addressed long-term-persistence creates a structural asymmetry that motivates the choice, but Arweave (200-year design), Filecoin (perpetual renewals), git (decades for major projects), Sigstore (Rekor transparency log for post-cert-expiry verification) all share that structural property and have NOT made Benten's choice. The §2.1 draft doesn't enumerate these comparable systems or explain WHY Benten differs from them — and that gap reads as either (a) Benten thinks it knows better than these established systems (which feeds Lens 5 small-team-overreach) OR (b) Benten hasn't fully thought through the class boundary (which feeds Lens 15 threat-model-boundaries). NARROWING THAT WOULD MAKE THE ARGUMENT DEFENSIBLE: explicitly enumerate the comparable-class systems (git/Sigstore/Filecoin/Arweave/Debian/permaweb) and articulate a SHARPER class boundary than 'content-addressed long-term-persistence' — because that boundary captures too much. Candidate sharper boundaries: (i) 'systems where the SIGNER is the principal AND the signature delegates capability that compounds over time' (UCAN-grant-chain semantics; not just signed-artifact-with-static-meaning like git commits); (ii) 'systems where signature verification is performed by third parties without out-of-band trust signals' (cuts the other way — git/Sigstore HAVE rich social trust signals: GitHub identity, Rekor transparency, web-of-maintainers; Benten's Atrium has weaker such signals at v1-beta); (iii) 'systems where a forged signature causes immediate authority delegation in an automated system without human review' (UCAN delegate-of-delegate chains; plugin manifest auto-install; AI-agent autonomous use per CLAUDE.md baked-in #18). Of these, (iii) is the SHARPEST defensible boundary because it lines up with Benten's specific use cases (plugin manifests, AI-agent autonomy at Phase-6) and gives a real reason why Sigstore/git/Arweave are NOT in the same class (human review is in the loop; forgery alone doesn't yield immediate authority). RECOMMENDED §2.1 REVISION: replace 'content-addressed long-term-persistence' with 'long-lived signatures that delegate capability into automated trust chains without per-use human review.' Concede explicitly that Sigstore/git/Filecoin/Arweave/Debian made the opposite choice and articulate why their threat model differs (in their case, signature consumption flows through human review at install/merge time + rich identity infrastructure; Benten's plugin manifests auto-load on every Atrium peer at every Drop sync). Also add a 'secondary trust factors' paragraph: an adversary forging a 2026-dated Drop in 2035 still has to either (a) sync it visibly into Atriums (detectable by canonical-replica divergence) OR (b) get downstream consumers to accept it via social trust signals (rotation logs, peer attestations, plugin-author Atrium presence). The §2.1 draft as written implies cryptographic signature is the sole trust factor; framing it as ONE factor among several (where PQ-hybrid raises the cost of attacking THIS factor) is more defensible than 'forging the signature wins.' IRRECOVERABLE HOLE IF NOT FIXED: with the current §2.1 framing, a skeptical reader will run the proves-too-much test in their head ('do I see git deprecating Ed25519? no. do I see Debian? no. do I see Filecoin? no. why is Benten special?') and conclude Benten is overreaching. That's the reputation-collapse failure-mode E in the plan.
